turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm a bit late. The van's half on the yellow lines and I was watching for a warden, and it's miserable rain out there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, sit yourself down. What have you come about?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the elbow. Pain on the outside of the right one, six weeks now, and I can't keep pretending it'll just go because the work doesn't stop.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right-handed for the painting, I assume?

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, right-handed. I hold the brush in the right, roller in the right, everything in the right, I did try switching for a ceiling once and the line went all wobbly so I gave that up.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Outer right elbow, six weeks, dominant arm. I'm already thinking this may be the tendon that works when you grip, rather than the joint proper. How did it begin?

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, no injury. I had a week of ceilings in a house in Didsbury, roller overhead the whole time, and it crept in, dull at first then sharper. I kept telling myself the weekend would sort it and the weekend didn't.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What sets it off now, in an ordinary day?

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Lifting a cup of tea, of all things. The mug, the kettle, a full tin of paint, and the gear stick in the van, that twist from second to third. Brush work I can start alright and then it builds and builds.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does the pain wake you at night?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Once I'm down it's quiet, sleep's been fine, I drop off with the radio same as always.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any tingling, or numbness, in the forearm or the hand?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, no, nothing like that. The hand's normal, I can feel the brush and the keys and the coins in my pocket, it's just the elbow itself.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you booked, I think your wife spoke to reception. What had she said was going on?

[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): She answered for me, yeah, I was up a ladder and couldn't come to the phone. She told them I can't grip a paintbrush at all, like the hand's packed in. That's not true. I can grip it, it burns after about twenty minutes, and if I push on the forearm aches, she's just dramatic.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the grip is there, it just hurts if you carry on. What are you taking for it?

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Neurofen, the four hundred milligram tablets, one three times a day, morning and lunch and when I get home. The lunch one I forget more often than not, if there's no water on site I just don't bother. And voltarol gel on the sore bit, morning and night.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So ibuprofen four hundred, aimed at three times a day, and diclofenac gel twice daily. Any allergies, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No allergies at all. I've had penicillin and I've had aspirin in the past, never a rash, never any swelling, nothing.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines you take regularly?

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing regular, no. They took my appendix out when I was twenty, keyhole, well I think it was the ordinary cut actually, long time ago, but I'm not on any tablets from that. Otherwise I'm fit, touch wood.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Appendix at twenty, nothing ongoing then. Any fever with this elbow?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No temperature, no shivers. My sister keeps texting me about infection, which is why I even thought of it, but no, I feel well in myself.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your weight, has that shifted?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. Not really. The jeans are a bit looser at the waist, but I skip breakfast on site and I haven't been on any scales, so I don't actually know if I've lost anything.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): No cough. Breathing's normal even on the ladders. Plaster dust makes me sniff, but that's not a cough, that's just the job.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. Family side, diabetes, heart disease, anything running through the family?

[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes, type two, it came on in his fifties and he was on tablets for years. My mother did not have diabetes, she never had sugar at all, though she died of a stroke at seventy-eight. My older sister June has high blood pressure and takes a tablet for the pressure, but she has no sugar, and my other sister Karen is fine, no pressure and no diabetes.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Useful, thank you. I want the work and the rest of the day as well, because a tendon complaint is half about hours and half about everything else, food, exercise, drink.

[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a painter and decorator, self-employed, twenty-odd years. Hours are long, six days most weeks, ten hours easy and twelve if the client's rushing, and I try to keep Sundays off. Diet's poor, bacon rolls and crisps from the van, hardly any veg, and I don't do a gym, the ladders are the only exercise I get. Drink is a couple of pints Friday and the same Saturday, three if there's a match, nothing in the week, and smoking I had the odd one in my twenties then packed it in, so not now.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heavy repetitive loading, six long days, the tendon barely gets a rest. I'll examine it now, say when it's tender.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, the hands are still painty, I did wash them, sort of.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's alright. Tender right over the lateral epicondyle, the bony point on the outside. Resisted wrist extension reproduces the pain in that same spot. There's no swelling, the elbow bends and straightens fully, and your grip in my hand is decent.

[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow, yes, that's the exact spot, easy. And I should correct myself, because I talked it down earlier. After a long day it does throb at night and it wakes me once or twice, and there's a fizzing tingling along the top of the forearm towards the wrist, not into the fingers. I didn't want it sounding worse than it is.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. OK, so there is night pain, and tingling over the forearm but not the hand. That changes the picture a little, though the tingling staying on the forearm matters.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, this is lateral epicondylitis, tennis elbow, the common extensor tendon pulling on that bone. I'm not calling it a neck or a trapped nerve, the pattern doesn't fit. It's a working impression from the story and the examination, not something a scan has proved.

[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): My mate Dave had a needle in his elbow, said it was magic for a month and then it came back worse, so are you doing an injection today? I've got a whole staircase to grain next week and I can't really be out of action, the client's already twitchy.

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): No injection today. If I put steroid into a tendon you're still hammering every day, I'm not convinced the benefit lasts, and there's a small chance of weakening the tendon. Physiotherapy and a brace first. If it hasn't settled after that, then we can consider an injection.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, a brace, like a strap? I saw one in Boots. Would I wear it driving as well, because of that gear stick, and all day or just for the heavy bits? I do go on, sorry.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): A tennis elbow clasp, worn snug during the heavier jobs, not every minute including driving if driving is light. I'll refer you for physiotherapy so they can load the tendon properly rather than just rest it. Pace the work, shorter stints, swap hands where the finish allows, don't take a month off. Ice for ten minutes after work, and keep the ibuprofen four hundred three times a day but with food, and stop it if your stomach burns.

[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Shorter stints, right. Mrs Kendal's landing is promised for Friday and a shop front on Monday, so I'll get the lad in for the ceilings. Ice, food with the tablets, I can do that. Do I keep the gel as well?

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, keep the gel morning and night, just don't put it on under a tight bandage. I don't think you need an x-ray, this isn't acting like a break or arthritis. I'll see you again in six weeks, and if the tingling spreads into the fingers or the arm goes weak, come back sooner rather than waiting.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks. If the physio takes ages to come through, do I still come, or only if I'm worse? They always say it's a long wait round here.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come at six weeks either way. That's a proper review, not only if you're worse. Reception will send the physio referral as you leave. The injection stays on the shelf unless this hasn't really moved by then.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Brilliant, that makes sense. I'll go and move the van before I get a ticket. Thanks for explaining it properly, I know I waffle.

spec.situation: Painter or carpenter with outer elbow pain for six weeks, worse lifting a cup; takes ibuprofen; physio and brace advice; no injection yet.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

bad.reason: Ibuprofen 400 mg for elbow pain is stated, but three-times-daily use is intended and often missed at lunch.

bad.reason: Conditional injection after brace/physio is supported, but it was requested by the patient, not the doctor.

omissions.text: Pain began gradually after a week of overhead ceiling work with a roller; there was no injury.
The patient is right-hand dominant and uses the right hand for painting/roller work.
Pain is triggered by gripping/lifting and twisting, and brush work starts tolerably then progressively builds.
Patient initially denied night pain and initially denied tingling/numbness in the forearm or hand before later correcting this.

The patient specifically denied hand numbness/tingling and said sensation in the hand was normal; later tingling was clarified as along the top of the forearm towards the wrist, not into the fingers/hand.
Reception/wife had reported he could not grip a paintbrush at all, but the patient corrected this: he can grip it, it burns after about 20 minutes, and pushing on causes forearm ache.
No regular medicines other than the ibuprofen and diclofenac gel.
No shivers/rigors with the elbow problem; he feels well in himself.
Weight change was uncertain rather than clearly absent: jeans are a bit looser, he skips breakfast, and he has not weighed himself so does not know if he has lost weight.
Family history negatives/extra details: mother did not have diabetes; older sister has no diabetes; other sister Karen has neither hypertension nor diabetes.
Doctor stated the pattern does not fit a neck problem or trapped nerve.
Doctor explicitly said no injection today and discussed that steroid injection may give non-lasting benefit and has a small risk of weakening the tendon if he continues heavy work.
Doctor advised not to wear the tennis elbow clasp every minute/all the time; wear it snug during heavier jobs, not necessarily for light driving.
Doctor said an x-ray is not needed because this is not behaving like a fracture or arthritis.
Doctor instructed the patient to come back at six weeks regardless, even if physiotherapy has not yet come through or he is not worse.
Reception will send the physiotherapy referral as the patient leaves.
